idiom_name: readonly interface descriptor + as-const catalogue + ReadonlyMap registry
implementation_notes: TypeScript erases its types at compilation, so a Type Object has to be a runtime value: declare a readonly interface for the descriptor, author the catalogue as data checked with as const / satisfies so typos in the file fail the build, and index it into a ReadonlyMap<string, MonsterType>. Typed objects hold the descriptor and delegate; the compiler checks the shape of your type data (the closest a language without runtime types gets to the paper's 'system provides its own type-checking rules'), while runtime validation of external JSON is a separate concern. The prototype machinery is the same one JavaScript uses - class syntax included - so there is one realization here, not two; discriminated unions with never-checks are the compile-checked alternative when the set of kinds is closed and the difference is behaviour.
pitfalls: Type erasure: the interface leaves no runtime trace, so validation of a JSON file loaded at startup must be done by a schema/validator or a hand-written guard; as-const/satisfies only checks data that is in the source.
Structural typing makes unrelated descriptors with the same shape mutually assignable - brand the descriptor type (& { readonly __brand: unique symbol }) when two kind families could be confused.

readonly is compile-time only: the objects in TYPES are ordinary mutable objects at runtime, so freeze them (Object.freeze) or keep the catalogue behind the ReadonlyMap so nothing can retune a shared type.
